title: Write a spec record
goal: An agent (or the owner) adds or changes a record under `specs/`: a domain rule, a use case and its requirements, a component, a test. The record is a file, so the change is reviewed in git like code.

title: Split a product into domains by capability
goal: The owner, or an agent, decides a product's domains before writing its records. Lathe's record format and its modeling skill steer each domain toward one business capability, a vertical slice that owns its records, rules, views, code and tests, and away from technology layers such as the web app or the server. `lathe check` warns of a domain named for a technology.

title: Change the meta-model
goal: The owner adds a kind of record or allows a new relation, for example a `glossary_term` kind, by editing `lathe/meta/*.csv`, and the change is reviewed in git like any other. A product changes its own meta-model the same way in its `metaExtensions` folder, adding kinds or widening Lathe's (`LA-AUT-UC04`). The app does not edit the meta-model. The next `lathe check` shows both records the change breaks and any mistake in the meta-model itself.

title: Adapt one of Lathe's default kinds in a product
goal: A product's specs do not quite fit a default kind, for example its domain rules sit directly under a domain rather than under an aggregate. Without forking Lathe, the person adds a row for that kind to the product's `metaExtensions` `kinds.csv` with only what changes, such as `domain` in `parent_kinds`. The next `lathe check` accepts the product's records, and every other default stays as it was.

title: Organize a domain's use cases into capabilities and patterns
goal: A domain has grown past a handful of use cases, and several of them share the same behavior. The person groups the domain's use cases into ordered **capabilities** (such as 01 Membership, 02 Catalog, 03 Lending) and moves the domain's flows and acceptance tests under the same capabilities, so that each capability is a slice through Define and Design. Behavior that several use cases share is written once as a **pattern** under the product, with named settings or none; each use case that follows it links it with `follows` and gives every setting a value, or `Not applicable:` and a reason, instead of restating its rules. A whole domain may follow a pattern too (LA-TRC-UC07). A rule that holds only for some values of a setting says so in `applies_when`. `lathe check` then reports a clashing or malformed order, a use case left outside the capabilities, a setting a use case has not given, and an `applies_when` that is malformed or names a setting the pattern lacks.
notes: Lathe checks only how patterns are used, not house rules about them: a rule such as "each aggregate has exactly one use case following its Record view pattern" is the product's own check (LA-CHK-UC05).

title: Write a flow as ordered steps and have them checked
goal: The owner, or an agent, writes a flow as `flow_step` records, as a real product writes its flows as tables: each step in order, with what happens, the view, endpoint or component it goes through, and what it carries out. `lathe check` says when two steps share a place, when a step carries out something its flow does not, and when the flow still claims something none of its steps does, so traceability can be read per step.

title: Cite records by the IDs a product writes
goal: A product's IDs do not always start with the product's ID. A real product's records may be `ACC-UC01`, `STD-04` and `SYS-C01`, so when only IDs with a product prefix were read, none of its citations were checked, while the bare product ID in any body counted as one. The person runs `lathe check`; the engine reads as a citation every token that is a record's ID, and every token that starts with a known prefix (a product's or a domain's ID, or an entry of `idPrefixes` in `lathe.config.json`). A bare product or domain ID counts only when written as a code span of its own. Only a token with a known prefix that no record has is reported as an unknown ID, so the warnings stay about real drift.

title: Read each kind's folder from the meta-model
goal: The owner, or an agent, reads which folder each kind sits in, as a real product lays out a domain's specs in stage folders (Define: Domain model, Use cases; Design: Interaction design, Technical specification, Test plan; and Shared for patterns), from `meta/sections.csv` and the `section` column of `kinds.csv`. A product can add a folder or move a kind into another with its extensions, and `lathe check` reports a kind whose folder is not listed or belongs to another stage.

title: Group components into layers
goal: The owner, or an agent, groups a domain's components into ordered layers, such as Models, Services and Web app, as a domain's use cases are grouped into capabilities. Each product names its own layers as records. `lathe check` reports a bad or repeated layer order, and a component left directly under a domain that has layers, and a component in a layer counts in its domain exactly as one directly under it.

title: Model each aggregate's entities and how they relate
goal: The owner, or an agent, writes each aggregate's records as entities: one root and its child parts, each with a Fields table, linked by `has_one`, `has_many` and `refers_to`, and puts a rule that holds across aggregates under the domain, naming with `involves` the aggregates it ties together. `lathe check` reports what keeps the ERDs from being drawn, and the app reads each entity's fields to draw a domain's ERD at aggregate level and each aggregate's own ERD.

title: Read the format reference generated from the meta-model
goal: The owner, or an agent, reads how every kind, relation, folder and check works without opening the CSVs or the SQL: `lathe format` writes the reference from the meta-model and the check files' header comments, after the product's extensions and with its own checks, and the app reads the same reference from `GET /api/format`. FORMAT.md keeps only the concepts, so a new kind or check needs no edit to it, and the `undocumented` check reports anything the reference would leave blank.

title: Model the domain events each aggregate raises
goal: The owner, or an agent, writes what happens in each aggregate as domain events: each under the aggregate that raises it, named in the past tense, with a Fields table of what it carries and, when an entity's change raises it, `raised_by` that entity. The records that react link to it with `reacts_to`. `lathe check` reports an event raised from another aggregate, an event that nothing reacts to and a title that does not read as past tense.

title: Write tests, flows and levels as a real product has them
goal: The owner, or an agent, converts a real product's specs into Lathe and keeps what that product already says, without a workaround that `lathe check` then reports as false errors and warnings. An engineering check `supports` the obligations it backs without proving them. A test that runs from a shared class in another file names that file in `key_file`. A flow with several paths names each step's `path`, and each path is numbered on its own. A domain rule about one entity sits under that entity, and a big layer holds sub-layers. A long list of requirements, interaction requirements or pattern rules is sorted into groups.

title: Read how each kind and check works, from where I am
goal: The Reader meets a kind or a check while reading the spec (a record's kind in the side bar, a problem's code, a required field) and opens what the format says about it in one step, without leaving the workbench. Each kind and each check has its own page, generated from the meta-model and the check files, so it is never out of date: a kind's place, fields, links and checks with a real example from the product, and a check's explanation with the problems it reports now. The record format's own page gives the concepts and an index of everything.

title: Open a record's file from the desktop app
goal: An author reveals the file behind the record in front, opens it in an editor or copies its ID, without leaving the desktop app.

title: Write the engineering standards the code follows
goal: The owner, or an agent, writes the rules the product's code follows, such as logging, error handling or naming, as a standard under the product with a `standard_rule` record for each rule. Each component or test that follows a rule links to it with `meets`, or cites its ID. A standard rule owes no coverage; `lathe check` warns of a rule that nothing meets or cites. A rule proved by tests stays a pattern rule: a rule you prove with tests is a pattern rule, and a rule you follow and cite is a standard rule. A reader finds the standards under Shared, beside the patterns.

title: Write how the system carries out a flow, as a technical flow
goal: The owner, or an agent, writes how the system carries out a flow as a technical flow, as a real product's technical specification does: ordered steps, each naming the component that does it, the transaction and locks it takes, and the obligations it designs. A step's `satisfies` counts as design, so an obligation designed in a step is not reported unsatisfied.

title: Group endpoints into APIs and write integrations
goal: The owner, or an agent, groups a domain's endpoints by resource into APIs, as a real product writes one API file per resource, and states once the rules and shapes every endpoint of an API shares. An outside system the domain exchanges with is an integration, with one interaction requirement per exchange, and a rule shared across the domain's interaction design sits under the domain.

title: Check the workspace from the command line
goal: After editing records or code, an agent runs `npm --prefix lathe run check` to find out whether the workspace is broken and what work is left, and fixes errors before handing the work back to the owner.

title: Add a check
goal: The owner decides on a new rule, and an agent adds it as a check so that every later load enforces it.

title: Find stale IDs cited in prose
goal: A record's body names other records by ID in its prose, such as a use case explaining which rule it relies on. When a record is renamed, split or removed, those citations go stale without anyone noticing, which is the most common drift in a real product's specs. The person runs `lathe check`; the engine reads the IDs each body cites outside code, keeps the ones that exist as the record's mentions for the app to show, and warns about each cited ID that no record has, so the wording can be fixed.

title: Find structural gaps and read each mistake once
goal: The owner, or an agent, runs `lathe check` on a product whose stages are written by different people at different times, and learns where they do not join up: a domain rule no use case relies on, a use case no flow carries out, an interaction requirement that carries out nothing, a test whose type does not suit what it proves, a component that satisfies nothing, a test that proves nothing. A product's extension can restate one of Lathe's relation rules in its own words without breaking. And when one record is wrong, for example a rule test given its rule's ID, the check says so once instead of in sixteen messages.

title: Add a product's own checks
goal: A product has house rules that Lathe should not impose on every product. One product, for example, requires each aggregate to have exactly one use case that follows its Record view pattern, and this repo requires every endpoint to state at least one interaction requirement. Lathe ships no such rule. Instead the owner, or an agent, names a `checks` folder in the product's `lathe.config.json` and writes each rule there as one SQL file, in the same form as Lathe's own checks. `lathe check` runs them after Lathe's checks and reports their problems with the others, so the product's rules live and change with the product.

title: Keep each level of the spec a useful size
goal: The owner, or an agent, keeps each level of a product's spec small enough to read and big enough to group something. `lathe check` warns when a record holds more children of one kind than the product's `structure.maxChildren` setting, and when a capability, a layer or a group holds only one record, counting a flow's steps per path and requirements and rules per group, so that a missing or needless level is found while the spec is written.

title: Review every problem of a product
goal: The owner looks at everything the checks found in one product, on its space's own Checks page, with the problems that belong to no product, to see what is broken before reviewing an agent's work.

title: Find a record in a domain
goal: The reader opens a domain to find a rule, use case, component or test, and to see what is missing.

title: Follow a record's links
goal: The reader reads one record and follows its links in either direction: from a requirement to the components that satisfy it and the tests that prove it, or from a test back to what it proves. To change a record the Owner edits it on its page (`LA-EXP-UC14`), or an Agent writes through the plugin's MCP tools; the page shows the change.

title: Walk the model as a graph
goal: The reader starts from any record, sees what it connects to, and walks the model by clicking from node to node, the way the record pages let them click from link to link. The graph is one map of the whole model that never changes shape: walking it is zooming in and out and centering, so the shape of a domain and its traceability read at a glance.

title: Walk the graph through folder-like groups
goal: The reader reads the graph like a folder tree: the domain, then "Use cases (5)", then each use case. A record with many children shows one group per kind of child, so they see what is there and how much, and focus only the group they want to walk into.

title: Read a record as a wiki page, a graph or a model, side by side
goal: The reader opens any record, group, domain or product at its one address and chooses how to read it, opening and closing views as panes side by side: as a page (Wiki), among its neighbors (Graph), and on a domain, aggregate or entity as an ERD (Model). Following a link in any pane moves them all, and the side bar beside them always shows the record's facts. They move around with a side navigation that folds away, find anything by ID or title, and read each page one level deep, opening only what they want.

title: Read a flow step by step
goal: The reader opens a flow and reads its steps in order as a table, as a real product's flow tables read: what happens at each step, the view, endpoint or component it goes through, and what it carries out. They unfold a step to read more. In the graph, the steps sit under their flow, and a requirement's trace shows the step that carries it out.

title: Work in one product at a time
goal: The reader works on one product at a time, as in one workspace at a time in Slack, Discord, Linear or Notion. A rail at the far left of the nav shows each product as a square icon; the reader chooses one and everything they see is that product's alone, as a separate space: the nav, quick find, its Checks, the graph, the Model view and the side bar. They switch with Alt+1 to Alt+9 (⌥1 to ⌥9 on a Mac) or from the command palette, and come back to the page they left.

title: Read a product laid out in stage folders
goal: The reader reads a product laid out in stage folders, the way a real product keeps its specs. In the side nav, under the current space, Shared holds the patterns; each domain folds into Define (Domain model, Use cases) and Design (Interaction design, Technical specification, Test plan), then its open questions. The domain page and the group pages use the same folders and names as headings, so the page and the nav match.

title: Read the technical specification and test plan in their groups
goal: The reader reads a domain's Technical specification and Test plan in groups instead of two long lists. Technical specification lists the domain's layers in order, each holding its components, then the components outside any layer. Test plan groups each test by its family and what it proves: acceptance tests by capability and use case, then domain rule, pattern, interaction and UI tests, design checks, then engineering checks. A sub-layer sits within its layer. The side nav, the domain page, the group pages and the graph all show the same groups, and the graph's trail names what the reader has visited.

title: Keep several records open in tabs
goal: The reader keeps several records, groups, domains or products open at once, as editors in VS Code, and flips between them without losing their place. A plain click opens a page in the preview tab, which the next plain click replaces; the reader keeps the tabs they want. Each tab keeps its own views, pane sizes, wiki scroll and graph settings, the address follows the active tab, and a reload brings them all back. The tabs sit at the left of the page bar above the panes; on a phone they are the Open pages sheet.

title: Read a domain and its aggregates as an ERD
goal: The reader opens the Model view on a domain and reads its domain model as an entity-relationship diagram: its aggregates and how their entities refer to each other. On an aggregate they read its entities with their fields and relationships, and on an entity the same diagram with that entity picked out. They also read cause and effect: the domain events each aggregate raises, the entity raising each, and the aggregates that react to them. They click a box to go to it, and read the key under the diagram for the colors, the line ends and the events.

title: Use the side bar for details, outline and history
goal: The Reader keeps a side bar at the right of the page, as VS Code's secondary side bar, and picks one of its three views from a small switcher at its top. Details describes what the Reader is pointing at or has selected in the graph, the Model view or the wiki, without repeating what the page already shows. Outline lists what the main view holds, the wiki's sections or the graph's records by level or the diagram's boxes, as rows to jump to. History lists the commits that changed the record's rows in the data files, the changes not committed yet first, each with what it changed. The side bar starts closed in the Wiki view, which shows a record's facts itself, and open in the Graph and Model views; each view mode and each tab keeps the Reader's own choice.

title: Read a domain's APIs, integrations and technical flows
goal: The reader opens a domain's API and reads its endpoints and the rules they all share, opens an integration and reads each exchange with its outside system, and finds both in Interaction design, and a technical flow in Technical specification beside its layer's components, as a real product's specs are laid out.

title: Change a record on its page
goal: The Owner, reading a record, fixes it where they read it: they edit its fields, its parent and its links in a form the schema shapes, add a child under it, or remove it after seeing what still names it. Each change is one write through the command layer, refused with its reasons when it breaks a rule, and lands in the data files as a small diff for review in git, as an Agent's writes do.

title: Load the workspace in code
goal: Code such as the web app's spec API, or an agent's script, calls `loadWorkspace(root)` to get every record, link, problem and coverage figure for the repo at `root`.

title: Set up Lathe in a product repo
goal: Lathe is installed into a product's own repo as a package, so the product's data files live beside its code and Lathe's improvements arrive with a version bump instead of by copying.

title: Trust that the page shows the files on disk
goal: While an agent changes records, the reader keeps the browser open and expects it to show what is in the data files now, and to say plainly when it is showing sample data instead.

title: Work the app from the keyboard
goal: The reader, used to VS Code and Claude Code, moves through the specs with the keys they already know: quick open, the command palette, toggling the side bars and views, going back, jumping to problems, and a sheet that lists every shortcut.

title: See each command's shortcut where it is used
goal: The reader learns the shortcuts the way they are learned in VS Code and Linear: by seeing them where they already click. A control's tooltip names it and its keys, the command palette shows each command's keys at the right of its row, and screen readers hear the keys too.

title: Arrange the workbench
goal: The reader sizes the navigation, the side bar and the open panes (Wiki, Graph, Model) to suit what they are reading, as in VS Code: they drag the gap between two panels, or focus it and use the keyboard. Lathe remembers the sizes, and dragging the navigation or the side bar small enough folds it away.

title: Choose and make a theme
goal: The reader picks how Lathe looks, as in VS Code: one of a few built-in themes (Lathe, High contrast, Workshop, Midnight and Graphite), and Light, Dark or the system's choice. They arrow through the themes and see each one at once. When none suits them, they duplicate one and change its colors, fonts, text size, density, corners, gaps and motion, with a warning wherever text gets hard to read, and share the result as a file.

title: Read and move around Lathe on a phone
goal: Away from a desk, the reader opens Lathe on a phone to read, not to arrange panels: they follow a record's links, check a domain's coverage, look at a graph or an ERD, and find a record by ID or title. One view fills the screen at a time; the nav, the side bar, the open pages and quick find come up as sheets and go away again; everything answers a thumb, and nothing needs a hover. On a tablet in landscape they keep the workbench, with targets sized for a finger. The decisions behind the design are in `notes/mobile-design.md`.

title: Read and move around without anything jumping
goal: The Reader opens pages, follows links, re-centers the graph, opens and closes panes, folds rows and resizes panels, and the specs reload under them as they change. Whatever changes, what the Reader is looking at stays where it was: the frame of the page holds still, new content takes the room kept for it, and anything that does move glides there on the shared motion. A header that grew with its title, a key that resized the diagram above it and a picture drawn once in the wrong place and then moved are the kind of jitter this rules out.

title: Use Lathe with a keyboard and a screen reader
goal: The Reader works without a mouse, or listens to the page through a screen reader, or both. They move through the nav, the page bar, the panes and the side bar with Tab and the arrow keys; open a record from the nav or quick find; switch views; re-center the graph; fold rows; show and hide the side bar; and pick a theme. Every control says what it is and what it does in words that match what is drawn, every part that scrolls can be reached, nothing holds focus, focus lands where the Reader expects after each move and comes back to where it was when a dialog or a sheet closes, and what changes out of sight is announced. The page reads as clearly in the High contrast theme, in light and dark, on a desk and on a phone. The findings behind the design are in `notes/a11y-audit.md`.

title: Open a product in a window
goal: The reader opens a product's folder, such as Lathe's own repo or another product's, and it opens in a window of its own with the product's name and folder in the title bar. Lathe in that window reads and live-reloads that folder, as in the browser. They come back to it from File › Open Recent, and the shell reopens the last folder when it starts.

title: Iterate on Lathe with hot reload in the desktop app
goal: The owner changes Lathe while using it in the desktop app. `npm --prefix desktop run dev` loads the app with hot reload: from the owner's own dev server on port 5199 when it serves the opened folder, so the browser and the shell share it, or from a dev server of the shell's own. Changing the shell itself restarts it, and record changes reload the page in every mode. When they want the app as it ships, they build it locally, unsigned.

title: Use Lathe from the native menus
goal: The reader uses the menu bar as in any Mac app: File to open folders and close windows, Edit, View for the app's views and the window's zoom and full screen, Window, and Help for the record format and the keyboard shortcuts. A menu choice runs the same command as its key in the app.

title: The desktop window looks like part of Lathe
goal: The reader works in a window with no system title bar, as in VS Code: the window's controls float over Lathe's own bar, drawn in the theme's colors. From the bar they go back and forward, see which page they are on and open quick find, and show or hide the navigation and the side bar. They drag the window by the bar and double-click it to zoom. When they change the theme or the light or dark mode, the bar and the window's controls follow.

title: Feel like a native Mac app
goal: The Owner keeps Lathe in the Dock like any well-made Mac app. Its icon reads at every size, in light and dark Docks, and a development build is marked DEV. The Dock badge counts the check errors of the space in front, and the Dock menu opens another product folder. About Lathe says which versions run, and Settings… opens the app's settings. From a record the Owner reveals the data file that holds its row in Finder, opens it in the editor or copies its ID, from the side bar or a right-click. Opening Lathe again, or a folder from Finder, goes to the running app. A window opens calmly on the shell color, says which product it is opening, and, when the engine cannot load the folder, says why and offers a way on.

title: Change the data through one command layer
goal: An Agent, through the plugin's MCP tools or the CLI, or the Owner, on a record's page, changes a product's records. Whichever writer they use, the change goes through the same command layer: it is checked whole against the schema, refused with every reason when it breaks a rule, and otherwise written to the data files as a small diff for review in git.

title: See a domain's coverage
goal: The owner asks how complete a domain is: how many of its obligations (requirements, domain rules, interaction requirements and any obligation kind the product adds) are designed (satisfied by a component), built (satisfied by a component whose file exists), proved (by an automated or manual test) and only planned, and which ones are not done. `LA-TRC-UC02` says how the meta-model decides what is counted.

title: Count coverage by the meta-model
goal: The owner sees coverage for every kind of obligation the product has, not only requirements and domain rules: interaction requirements at views, endpoints and flows, and any obligation kind the product adds to the meta-model. For each domain and obligation kind they see how many are designed, built, proved, and only planned.

title: Record how a test proves its obligations
goal: A person writes a `test` record for each test that proves a requirement, domain rule or other obligation, and says how it runs with `state`:
notes: `lathe check` reports a test whose state, `run_by` or file does not fit.

title: Prove the rules of the patterns a domain follows
goal: A pattern states behavior that several use cases share. Its rules are written once, as `pattern_rule` records under the pattern, instead of in its body. Every domain that follows the pattern (the domain itself or one of its use cases `follows` it) must prove each rule in its own tests, as a real product's "Patterns we follow" tables do: proof in one domain says nothing about another. Pattern rules need proof only by default; a product that sets `pattern_rule` to `obligation: yes` asks for each rule's design in the domain's own components too. A rule that depends on a setting names it, and a domain that follows only through use cases that all mark that setting `Not applicable:` with a reason does not owe the rule. A rule that applies only for some values of a setting says so in `applies_when`, and is waived, neither owed nor proved, in a domain where no follower gives a value that meets it.
notes: The person writes the rules under the pattern, links each following domain's tests to them with `proves` (and its components with `satisfies`, where design is asked or wanted), and runs `lathe check`. Coverage shows one Pattern rule line per domain; the gaps and the `unproved` (and, where design is asked, `unsatisfied`) warnings name the rule and the domain that still owes it. A pattern nobody follows, a rule naming a setting its pattern does not have, and any other obligation that sits in no domain are reported.

title: Check every proof a test claims
goal: A test record says which records it proves. A person, or an AI agent, writes the test and its code, and `lathe check` confirms that the code backs every claim:
notes:
The person fixes each error by naming the missing ID in the test's name, by naming the test's own ID, or by removing a claim the test does not really prove.

A claim the code does not back proves nothing: its obligation stays unproved, in the `unproved` warnings and in coverage alike.

title: See proof still owed and each domain's tests by state
goal: The owner, or an agent, runs `lathe check` or reads the workspace's coverage and learns how much proof is still owed by tests not written yet, including for obligations another test already proves, and how many tests each domain has by state: automated, manual and planned, as a real product's test-coverage table counts them.

title: Follow a pattern per domain, with or without settings
goal: A real product adopts most of its patterns for a whole domain, writes several with no settings, and asks only for proof of their rules. The owner, or an agent, links a domain to a pattern with `follows` and leaves `settings` out where a pattern has none. Coverage then counts each rule in that domain, as it does for a domain whose use cases follow the pattern, and asks only for proof: a pattern rule needs no component, since a real product often builds it through shared helpers. A use case that follows a pattern needs no requirements of its own, and interaction requirements and flow steps may fulfill pattern rules directly, with `flow-step-fulfills-outside-flow` treating the rules of the patterns a flow's use cases or domain follow as inside the flow. A product that wants pattern rules designed too sets `pattern_rule` back to `obligation: yes` in its extension, and any kind may be made proof-only with `obligation: proof`.

title: Name owed proofs and report proofs that count nowhere
goal: The owner, or an agent, runs `lathe check` and reads, by ID, each proved obligation that a planned test still owes a proof of, as a real product lists the pattern proofs still needed; each test whose proof counts in no domain's coverage, with the reason for each target; and each manual test whose `run_by` file never mentions it.

title: See each domain's coverage and the product's summary
goal: The reader opens a product to see its domains, how complete each one is (designed, built and proved), what is still undecided and what is broken.

title: Trace a requirement in the graph
goal: The reader picks a requirement or domain rule and switches the graph to its traceability chain alone: what fulfills it, which components satisfy it, which tests prove it, and the files they name. Gaps in the chain show at once.

title: See every obligation kind and test state
goal: The reader reads coverage for every kind of obligation the meta-model names (requirements, domain rules, interaction requirements and any kind the product adds), finds each interaction requirement at the view, endpoint or flow it belongs to, and tells at a glance which tests are automated, which are manual and which are only planned.

title: See the patterns a domain follows and the rules it owes
goal: The reader opens a domain and sees which patterns its use cases follow, and for each pattern rule whether the domain designs, builds and proves it, marks it not applicable, or has it waived, as a real product's "Patterns we follow" tables do. They open a pattern to see its settings, its rules and who follows it. Reading any record, they follow the IDs its prose cites with one click, and see at a glance which cited IDs no longer exist.

title: See proof still owed and tests by state with each domain's coverage
goal: The reader reads a product's or a domain's coverage and sees, beside the planned bar, how many obligations already proved still have a planned test, so planned proof is not hidden by other tests. With each domain's coverage they read its tests by state, and the product's summary totals them, as a real product's test-coverage table does.

title: See what designs, proves and carries out a record
goal: The Reader opens a record and, below its body, reads its Traceability: for a requirement or rule, the components that design it (each marked built or not), the tests that prove it (each with its state), the tests that support it, and the flows, views and endpoints that carry it out, with a callout for each gap coverage finds. A use case shows its requirements in a table of Designed, Built and Proved. A component shows what it satisfies and the tests that prove those things; a test shows what it proves and the file that runs it. Every list is titled by its links' label, read from this record, as are the record facts, the side bar, the graph and the Model view.
